h.1: Head to the Cheboksary Bay waterfront and face the water.
h.2: Head to Bondarev Street — the fortress’s east wall ran along here.
h.3: Head to Vvedensky Cathedral on Konstantin Ivanov Street.
q.1: According to Olearius, how many people gathered on the riverbank to meet the embassy?
q.2: According to the 1613 inventory, how many towers did the town have?
q.3: How many apostles are depicted on the cathedral’s Royal Doors?
r.1: That’s right — about three hundred, young and old.
r.2: That’s right — five towers, two of them gates: Vvedensky and Nikolsky.
r.3: That’s right — eleven, not twelve. A rare feature of these mid-1700s doors.
today.1: Today this is the Cheboksary Bay waterfront.
today.2: Today: Bondarev and Sverdlov Streets. The wall has been gone for more than three hundred years.
art.A1_KRESALO.name: Fire striker
art.A1_KRESALO.desc: 1400s. Iron. Found in Cheboksary during the 1969–1970 dig. Struck against flint to make a spark.
art.A2_VESLO.name: Oar
art.A2_VESLO.desc: 1400s–1600s. Wood. About three feet long, with a blade of 28–35 cm. Seven oars like this turned up in the Cheboksary dig.
art.A3_BERESTA.name: Birch-bark vessel with an inscription
art.A3_BERESTA.desc: Early 1500s. Birch bark. A fragment of the inscription “БЕРЕЗОВЫЙ ЛЕ…” and a pattern like those in handwritten books. Found in Cheboksary in 1969.
art.A4_ZERKALO.name: Bronze mirror
art.A4_ZERKALO.desc: 1300s. Bronze. A small mirror with a pattern of raised bumps, typical of the Golden Horde era. Found in Cheboksary.
art.A5_BERDYSH.name: Berdysh (poleaxe)
art.A5_BERDYSH.desc: 1600s. Iron. Blade 70 cm, weight 800 g. Found in the Cheboksary district. The berdysh was the streltsy’s weapon.
art.A6_IZRAZETS.name: Green glazed stove tile
art.A6_IZRAZETS.desc: 1600s. Clay, green glaze. Tiles like this covered the stoves. Found in Cheboksary.
art.A7_KOPEYKA.name: Silver kopeck
art.A7_KOPEYKA.desc: 1615–1645, Tsar Mikhail Fyodorovich. Silver, 0.48 g. A typical coin of the time; a 1500s–1600s silver kopeck was found in Cheboksary in 2025.
ui.share_text: I finished “Town by the Water” in the game Na Cheboksare and collected real finds from the Cheboksary digs.
ui.title: NA CHEBOKSARE
ui.splash_quote:
“…they spent the night at Cheboksar, and from Cheboksar they marched all day and all night and reached Kazan at the break of dawn.”
Chronicle, 1469
h.4: Go to the Yefremov mansions on Konstantin Ivanov Street — today they house the Chuvash National Museum.
h.5: Go down to the water, to the old wharf — where the grain boats once came in.
h.6: Walk along the bay embankment: the gymnasium stood on Naberezhno-Arkhangelskaya Street, later Chernyshevsky Street.
h.7: Climb Vladimir Hill to the Transfiguration Convent; the Yefremov tomb is on the slope, entrance from the north.
h.8: Walk along the parapets of Cheboksary Bay and look for the little figures.
today.4: Today the Yefremov mansions are museums.
today.5: Today this is the embankment and the bay — the barns are long gone.
today.6: Today this is the Cheboksary Bay embankment.
today.7: The convent is active today; the tomb is the parish church of St John of Kronstadt.
today.8: Today this is the townspeople”s favorite promenade.
q.4: How many sacks a year did the Yefremovs” bast-sack workshop make?
r.4: Correct — up to thirty thousand sacks: thirty adults and sixty youngsters.
q.5: According to the governor”s report, how many barns with grain and provisions burned in the fire of 1773?
r.5: Correct — forty-nine. And twenty-nine churches and seven hundred and seventeen houses besides.
q.6: How many girls came to the pro-gymnasium”s first lessons in October 1904?
r.6: Correct — forty-six. Every one of them had passed the entrance examination.
q.7: In what year was the convent on Vladimir Hill reborn?
r.7: Correct — on 25 March 1991, as the Transfiguration Convent.
q.8: How many figures of legendary heroes stand on the parapets of the bay?
r.8: Correct — six. And one of them is me.

art.A8_TORGOVY_DOM.name: Trading house “P. Ye. Yefremov and Sons”
art.A8_TORGOVY_DOM.desc: 1906. Founded with a capital of 325,000 roubles; managing partner Nikolai Yefremov. Evidence from the Chuvash Encyclopaedia.
art.A9_DOKLAD_1773.name: Report on the fire of 1773
art.A9_DOKLAD_1773.desc: The Kazan governor von Brandt”s report to the Senate: 29 churches, 717 houses, 49 barns. Evidence from the study module “Secrets of the Ancient Kremlin”.
art.A10_PORTRETY_1908.name: The Yefremov portraits in the pro-gymnasium
art.A10_PORTRETY_1908.desc: 1908. By decision of the town council, portraits of the honorary patroness Yekaterina Yefremova and her husband Prokopy were placed in the pro-gymnasium. Evidence.
art.A11_PROEKT_1907.name: Design of the tomb, 1907
art.A11_PROEKT_1907.desc: Architects K. S. Oleshkevich, M. Ya. Deminev, F. N. Malinovsky. The chapel was built in 1908–1911. Evidence from the Chuvash Encyclopaedia.
art.A12_FIGURKI.name: The six figures of the bay
art.A12_FIGURKI.desc: The Girl on the Moon, the Dancing Fox, Plagi the Beauty, Volga, Ulyp the Bogatyr, Narspi and Setner. Game find: all six found.

T00_PROLOG: The army of Voivode Ivan Run was marching on Kazan. The chronicle records: “…they spent the night at Cheboksar, and from Cheboksar they marched all day and all night and reached Kazan at the break of dawn.” These are the earliest words about our town that have come down to us.
T01_OLEARIUS:
By evening we arrived at the town of Cheboksary, lying forty versts from the settlement we had encountered the day before on the right bank. Like the two before it, this town is also built of wood; in its layout and its houses it is the most pleasant to look at of the three.
When the townspeople, even before we arrived, saw our large ship from a distance, they wondered what it could be. So the voevoda sent a boat with streltsy to meet us — three versts from town, near Mokritsa Island — to find out and see what sort of people we were. The soldiers rowed around the ship from a distance and hurried back to town.
When our passport was delivered into the town, three hundred people, young and old, ran out to the riverbank to look at us.
T02_NAGOY:
That same summer, a town was built at Cheboksary. The voevodas posted at Cheboksary for the year were: the okolnichy Vasily Petrovich Borisov, Fyodor Mikhailovich Nagoy, and Prince Vasily Semyonovich Funikov. Outside the town — Osip Vasilyevich Polev.
Archbishop Gury of Kazan blessed this place and set up an icon of the Most Pure Mother of God to watch over the town.
T03_ROSPIS_1613: Inventory of the town of Cheboksary, August 9, 1613. The town has five towers, two of which are gate towers — the Vvedensky Gate and the Nikolsky Gate. The stockade has four towers.
T04_KREMLIN_NARR:
The town on this slope was founded in the summer of 1555. But people lived here long before that: archaeologists found layers of settlement nearly five meters deep, spanning thirteen periods of construction. The oldest traces go back to the 1200s and 1300s — two 1300s potters’ workshops and a jeweler’s workshop with three smelting furnaces, where they even worked with gold; bronze and bone combs, a bronze mirror from the Golden Horde era, and a birch-bark vessel with a Russian inscription from the early 1500s.
The fortress’s east wall ran where Bondarev Street is today. And even in the 1800s, the way down Sverdlov Street followed the line of the old moat to the bay. Walk it — you’re walking alongside a wall that’s been gone for over three hundred years.
T05_SOBOR_NARR:
This cathedral was built by local masons working under master builders from Nizhny Novgorod. Brickmaking had to be set up in town for the first time just for this building — there were no stone buildings here before.
Look at the south wall: that’s the Akathist to Sweetest Jesus, a subject that is extremely rare in wall painting. In 1912 the parish asked for permission to paint over these murals. The Imperial Archaeological Commission said no — and the paintings survived.
Now find the Royal Doors and count the apostles.
T06_EFREMOV_NARR:
This whole block was built by one family. Its founder, Yefrem Yefimov, was a state peasant from the village of Shinerposi: he began with a cottage trade and grain dealing, and in the 1840s moved to Cheboksary with his son Prokopy and set up a trading firm.
Prokopy Yefremov rose from a peasant with a trading license to a merchant of the first guild. The Yefremovs sold flour in St Petersburg, Nizhny Novgorod and Rybinsk; they owned the three most powerful mills in the district and the largest bast-sack workshop in town — thirty adults and sixty youngsters made up to thirty thousand sacks a year. In 1890 the brothers opened a sawmill, and in 1906 the trading house “P. Ye. Yefremov and Sons”. Their total turnover reached half a million roubles a year.
Their money ran a free canteen during the Russo-Japanese War, opened an orphanage, bought the building for the girls” pro-gymnasium and kept the town library going. Their son Fyodor was mayor in 1914–1917; their son Nikolai sat in the State Duma. Between their houses stood warehouses, shops, gardens, hothouses and orangeries. Today the Yefremov mansions house the Chuvash National Museum and the Russian Art Department of the Art Museum.
T07_FONBRANT: “On the 30th day of April there was a fire in the town of Cheboksary, in which there burned 29 churches, 717 townspeople”s houses… storehouses on the wharves, barns with grain and other provisions — 49… trading stalls with sundry goods — 38.”
T08_AMBARY_NARR:
Here by the water stood the town”s wealth — the grain barns. In 1743 fifty-five of them were counted, and by the mid-nineteenth century some thirty barns on the wharf held up to a hundred and twenty thousand chetverts of grain. Rye and flour in bast sacks were kept until the price was right, then loaded onto barges — and off up the Volga. Already in the mid-eighteenth century two thirds of Cheboksary”s grain went to St Petersburg, where it fetched three to four times the price it did here.
Grain made the merchants cunning. Prices were written on goods in letters — each kept his cipher as a great secret. Peasant carts were intercepted on the roads into town so that no honest price could form on the square. In 1833 the town governor Kropotkin had the side streets barricaded, so that every cart passed the guards.
On 30 April 1773 a fire took twenty-nine churches and seven hundred and seventeen houses. The merchant Klyuyevs lost goods worth three thousand one hundred roubles. The merchant”s son borrowed money and began buying grain again — and ten years later nearly thirty thousand roubles were turning over in his hands. Fire and rebirth: that is how this shore lived.
T09_GIMNAZIA_NARR:
It took the town eight years to open a school for girls. The council first planned a pro-gymnasium in 1896, but the treasury never sent the money. In 1904 the town board bought a two-story stone house on Naberezhno-Arkhangelskaya Street from the merchant”s widow Zabrodina — the ten thousand roubles were borrowed from merchants, the first of them Prokopy Yefremov. In mid-October forty-six girls who had passed the entrance examinations began their lessons. The whole staff: a headmistress, two teachers and a scripture teacher.
There was no boarding house: in 1907 a hundred and fifty-nine pupils lived in groups in twenty-two private lodgings, and the teachers made the rounds of their homes. They studied scripture, Russian and Church Slavonic, arithmetic and geometry, German and French, penmanship, drawing, singing and needlework. From 1908 the pro-gymnasium became a full gymnasium, and by 1914 three hundred and five girls studied here. One of the district council”s scholarship girls was O. I. Yrzem — a future People”s Artist of the Chuvash republic.
In 1918 the gymnasium was turned into a Soviet secondary school. Zabrodina”s house later held a teacher-training college and the agricultural institute, and the street was renamed after Chernyshevsky.
T10_GORKA_NARR:
This hill is the quietest corner of the old town. From the eighteenth century the Vladimir hermitage stood here, and in 1899 a Chuvash women”s community was opened in its place. By the early twentieth century there were a church with three altars, a hospital with a wooden chapel, icon-painting and metal-chasing workshops, a garden and a pond, and from 1900 a school for orphan girls. Up to a hundred and fifty sisters gathered here.
On the slope, in 1908–1911, the Yefremov family tomb was built to a design by the architects Oleshkevich, Deminev and Malinovsky — a stone chapel with a dome and a Corinthian portico, the only monument of memorial architecture in Chuvashia. Until 1918 the sarcophagi of Prokopy Yefremov and his wife Yekaterina stood in its crypt.
In 1920 a children”s home was opened in the community”s buildings; in 1930 the church too was closed. Later there were flats here, a cooper”s shop, warehouses and restoration workshops. In 1989 the church was returned to the faithful, and on 25 March 1991 the convent was reborn — now as the Transfiguration Convent. That same year the tomb became the parish church of St John of Kronstadt.
T11_FIGURKI_NARR:
The bay you see is younger than anything we have talked about: its first section was filled in 1980, and the dam and fountains were built in 1996. The seven fountains are not decoration but an outlet: that is how Volga water is fed into the bay. The big one throws four jets twenty meters high; the six small ones stand around it in a circle.
And on the parapets of the bay live six little figures of heroes from Chuvash legends: the Girl on the Moon, the Dancing Fox, Plagi the Beauty, Volga, Ulyp the Bogatyr, and a pair — Narspi and Setner. They were installed in 2024. Narspi and Setner come from Konstantin Ivanov”s poem; the others from the project “Legends of the Chuvash Land”.
Find all six. I am that very Setner — so you already know one of them by sight.
L01_VYRODKOV: “The story goes that the Tsar sent a clever clerk, Ivan Vyrodkov, the man who built the town at Sviyazhsk in a month. People say he had a hand in ours too. But there’s no paper left about it — not one line. Maybe he was never here at all.”
L02_GOD_1469: “Some chroniclers write that the voivodes camped here for the night in the year 6977 — that’s 1469 the way we count. Others say a year later. Give or take a year, the town has been standing ever since.”
L03_TORAMUSH: “The icon Archbishop Guriy brought, we call it by our own name — Toramush. Турӑ амӑшӗ, the Mother of God. You won’t find that name in the books, but people still use it.”
L04_POZHAR: “The wooden church the Archbishop built burned down. Some say it was in ’49, others say ’59. And where it stood, a stone church went up.”
L05_MERA: “They say the wall ran almost a verst all the way around. Over two sazhens high and nearly two thick. I never measured it myself — that’s just what the old-timers say.”
L06_GOD_SOBORA: “They say the stone church went up in ’51. But about ten years later the Dutchman Witsen drew our town — and there’s no church in his drawing. Either he was sloppy, or we’ve got the year too early.”
L07_FRESKI: “Some say these paintings are old, made in Tsar Alexei’s time. But the one who tested the paint says they’re a century younger. The scholars argue, and the walls stay silent.”
L08_VOEVODA: “Who counts as our first voivode is argued too. The document names all three at once: okolnichy Borisov, Fyodor Nagoy, and Prince Funikov — serving the same year together. Who to call first — by rank in the list, or some other way — that’s up to you.”
